name: Hampton University
description: Founded in 1868 by the American Missionary Association under former Union general Samuel Chapman Armstrong, on ground where Mary S. Peake had taught freedpeople beneath the Emancipation Oak since 1861. Hampton's industrial-education model trained Booker T. Washington and shaped Tuskegee and dozens of other schools. Its alumni run deep in Black business history — from Chicago Defender founder Robert S. Abbott to Oracle president Charles Phillips (MBA) and Baltimore Ravens president Sashi Brown.

facts.d: The university dates its origins to September 17, 1861, when Mary S. Peake began teaching freedmen for the American Missionary Association.
Hampton held Virginia's land-grant program for Black students until 1920, when it moved to Virginia State.
The Hampton University Museum is described as the oldest African diaspora museum in the United States.
Robert S. Abbott (1896) and his nephew John H. Sengstacke (1934) — the two men who built and ran the Chicago Defender — both studied at Hampton.

sources.label: Hampton University School of Business — Notable Alumni

name: Virginia State University
description: Chartered by the Virginia legislature on March 6, 1882, as the Virginia Normal and Collegiate Institute, it is described as the first fully state-supported four-year institution of higher learning for Black Americans; John Mercer Langston was its first president. It became Virginia's 1890 land-grant HBCU when the program moved from Hampton in 1920. Its business school is named for alumnus Reginald F. Lewis, the TLC Beatrice financier.

facts.d: Opened October 1, 1883 after a lawsuit delayed it 19 months; 126 students and seven faculty in year one.
The federal land-grant program for Black Virginians moved from Hampton Institute to the school in 1920.

facts.t: Reginald F. Lewis College of Business.
facts.d: The business college carries the name of its 1965 alumnus, described by the school as 'America's First Black Billionaire Businessman'.
Received $30 million in 2020 and $50 million in 2025 — the largest single gift in its history.

sources.label: VSU Reginald F. Lewis College of Business — Alumni

name: Norfolk State University
formerNames: Norfolk Unit (Division) of Virginia Union University
description: Opened September 18, 1935, as the Norfolk Unit of Virginia Union University with about 85 students, it became independent in 1942, was folded into Virginia State College in 1944, and separated again in 1969. Today it is Virginia's largest HBCU by many measures, with a School of Business whose entrepreneurship institute bears the name of auto-dealer alumnus Ernest M. Hodge.

facts.t: Born as a Virginia Union branch.
facts.d: Founded in 1935 as the Norfolk Unit of Virginia Union University; renamed Norfolk Polytechnic College in 1942.
Separated from Virginia State and gained SACS accreditation in 1969; university status in 1979.
The Ernest M. Hodge Institute for Entrepreneurship honors the 1975 business graduate who built one of the largest Black-owned auto dealership groups.
Received $40 million (2020) and $50 million (2025) gifts.

sources.label: NSU — Ernest M. Hodge Institute for Entrepreneurship

connections.label: began as Norfolk Unit of VUU, 1935

name: Virginia Union University
affiliation: American Baptist Home Mission Society; American Baptist Churches USA
description: Founded in 1865 by the American Baptist Home Mission Society to train freedmen for ministry, it met for a time in the former Lumpkin's Jail slave pen. Virginia Union formed in 1899 when Richmond Theological Seminary merged with Washington's Wayland Seminary; Hartshorn Memorial College joined in 1932 and Storer College's endowment in 1964. It produced Governor L. Douglas Wilder, Pittsburgh Courier publisher Robert L. Vann, and the Richmond bankers who ran Consolidated Bank and Trust.

facts.d: From 1867 the school was housed in the building long known as Lumpkin's Jail.
Richmond Theological Seminary and Wayland Seminary merged to form Virginia Union University; first classes met October 4, 1899.
Hartshorn Memorial College merged in 1932 (making VUU coeducational) and Storer College merged its assets in 1964.
Norfolk State began in 1935 as VUU's Norfolk Unit.

name: Richmond Theological Seminary
fate: Merged with Wayland Seminary in 1899 to form Virginia Union University.
description: The Richmond branch of the ABHMS's National Theological Institute, holding classes by November 1865 and from 1867 meeting in Lumpkin's Jail under Nathaniel Colver. Incorporated as Richmond Institute in 1876 and re-established as Richmond Theological Seminary in 1886, it trained early Black Baptist leaders such as businessman-educator James H. Blackwell (1880).

facts.d: Nathaniel Colver resumed the school in 1867 in the former slave-trading jail.
Joined Wayland Seminary to create Virginia Union University.

name: Wayland Seminary
fate: Merged with Richmond Theological Seminary in 1899 to form Virginia Union University.
description: The Washington, D.C. branch of the ABHMS National Theological Institute, named for Baptist educator Francis Wayland and led for 30 years by George Mellen Prentiss King. It received a Freedmen's Bureau grant and counted Booker T. Washington among its students (1878–79).

facts.d: Received a $1,500 grant from the Freedmen's Bureau.
Moved its work to Richmond to form Virginia Union University.

name: Hartshorn Memorial College
fate: Merged into Virginia Union University in 1932, making VUU coeducational.
description: Founded in Richmond in 1883 as a college for African American women under Baptist sponsorship. For nearly half a century it educated Black women teachers and missionaries before merging into neighboring Virginia Union.

facts.d: Established specifically for African American women.
Its merger made Virginia Union coeducational.

name: Virginia University of Lynchburg
description: Organized in May 1886 at the 19th annual session of the Virginia Baptist State Convention, it was founded and run by Black Baptists rather than a white missionary society — an early model of Black institutional self-reliance. Civil-rights forerunner Vernon Johns graduated in 1915 and later served as its president.

facts.d: Organized by the Black Virginia Baptist State Convention in 1886.
The 1915 graduate served as president 1929–1933 before leading Montgomery's Dexter Avenue Baptist Church.

connections.label: founded by Virginia Baptist State Convention, 1886

name: Saint Paul's College
formerNames: Saint Paul Normal and Industrial School
fate: Lost SACS accreditation over finances and faculty credentials; after a planned merger with Saint Augustine's fell through in May 2013, it closed June 30, 2013.
description: Founded in 1888 by Hampton-trained Episcopal priest James Solomon Russell, who had begun teaching in a church room in 1883, as Saint Paul Normal and Industrial School. At its peak about 1,000 students attended; by closing it had about 150, and the campus was later sold.

facts.d: James Solomon Russell bought the first building with a legacy from the Rev. Saul of Philadelphia.
SACS revoked accreditation; a court injunction briefly reinstated probation before trustees chose to close.
The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation sold most of the campus in 2017 for $2.5 million.

sources.label: Episcopal News Service — St. Paul's College to close (2013)
Diverse Issues in Higher Education — After 125 years, St. Paul's shutting down
Lost Colleges — St. Paul Normal and Industrial School

name: Bishop Payne Divinity School
fate: Closed in 1949; its work for Black Episcopal clergy was absorbed by the (historically white) Virginia Theological Seminary in Alexandria.
description: An Episcopal school in Petersburg that trained Black clergy for the church in the South; it began as a normal and industrial school and did not award bachelor's degrees until 1910. Saint Paul's College founder James Solomon Russell studied here from 1878.

facts.d: Founded 1878 in Petersburg.
Admitted in 1878; went on to found Saint Paul's College.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Wilberforce University
description: Founded in 1856 by the Methodist Episcopal Church with AME participation and named for abolitionist William Wilberforce; in 1863 the AME Church under Bishop Daniel A. Payne bought it, making it the first college owned and operated by African Americans. Its alumni include Parks Sausage CEO Raymond V. Haysbert, golf-course pioneer Bill Powell, and Lewis College of Business founder Violet T. Lewis.

facts.d: Purchased by the AME Church in 1863 under Bishop Daniel Payne.
A state-funded Combined Normal and Industrial Department, created on its campus in 1887, became Central State University.
Wilberforce's golf team, including future Clearview owner Bill Powell, played Ohio Northern in 1937.
Opened a center for entrepreneurship named for alumni Mark and Shelly Wilson.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Wilberforce opens new center for entrepreneurship

name: Central State University
formerNames: Combined Normal and Industrial Department of Wilberforce University
College of Education and Industrial Arts
description: Began in 1887 as a state-funded department on Wilberforce University's campus and separated in 1947, becoming Central State College (1951) and University (1965); Ohio's only public HBCU, it gained 1890 land-grant status in 2014. Graduates include MAXIMA Corp. founder Joshua I. Smith, BET executive Curtis Symonds and opera star Leontyne Price.

facts.d: Created by the Ohio legislature in 1887 as a department of Wilberforce; independent from 1947.
Designated an 1890 land-grant institution in 2014.
Inducts alumni each Charter Day, including Leontyne Price (1948) in 2025.

sources.label: Central State — 138th Charter Day Convocation (Hall of Fame)
Wikipedia — Raymond V. Haysbert (attended Central State & Wilberforce)

connections.label: began as state department of Wilberforce, 1887

name: Payne Theological Seminary
description: The AME Church's seminary, named for Bishop Daniel A. Payne and established on land adjacent to Wilberforce University, carrying on the theological work that dates to Wilberforce's 1856 founding. It is the oldest freestanding African American theological seminary and trains clergy for the AME connection.

facts.d: Honors the AME bishop who bought Wilberforce for the church in 1863.
Appears on the federal-style lists of current HBCUs in Ohio alongside Wilberforce and Central State.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

connections.label: grew out of Wilberforce's theology work

name: Pensole Lewis College of Business & Design
description: Violet T. Lewis, a Wilberforce-trained businesswoman, opened Lewis Business College in Indianapolis in 1928 on a $50 loan and opened a Detroit branch around 1938–39; it was Michigan's only HBCU. After losing accreditation and a long decline it closed around 2013–2015, then was revived in 2021–22 by designer D'Wayne Edwards as Pensole Lewis College — described as the first closed HBCU ever to reopen.

facts.d: Violet T. Lewis opened the school in January 1928 in Indianapolis.
Sources differ on whether the Education Department designated it an HBCU in 1957 or 1987.
Rebranded in 2021 and re-established under Michigan legislation; was pursuing new accreditation in partnership with the College for Creative Studies.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Pensole Lewis College of Business and Design
TPInsights — First closed HBCU to reopen

name: Western University
fate: Lost funding in the Great Depression and competition for students; closed in 1943. Only a John Brown statue remains of the campus.
description: Began as the Quindaro Freedman's School in the free-state river town of Quindaro, an Underground Railroad stop, and became Western University in 1881 when the AME Church took it over. Its music department was celebrated: alumni included choral pioneer Eva Jessye and singer-actress Etta Moten Barnett.

facts.d: The only HBCU in Kansas history; state funds supported its industrial department.
Will Marion Cook taught there; Eva Jessye, Nora Douglas Holt and Etta Moten Barnett studied there.
Only the John Brown statue in front of the former Ward Hall survives.

sources.label: Community Voice — Quindaro Freedman's School was Kansas's HBCU

name: Lincoln University of Missouri
description: Founded in 1866 by Black Union veterans of the 62nd and 65th U.S. Colored Infantry, who pooled their pay to start Lincoln Institute. It became Missouri's 1890 land-grant school and was at the center of Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938). Business alumni include restaurant franchise mogul Valerie Daniels-Carter, barbecue king Ollie Gates and Walmart heiress Ann Walton Kroenke.

facts.d: Soldiers of the 62nd and 65th U.S. Colored Infantry funded the school in 1866.
Black Enterprise identifies nursing graduate Ann Walton Kroenke, a billionaire Walmart heir, as the wealthiest HBCU graduate.
Valerie Daniels-Carter (1978) keynoted the 2026 Founders' Day.

name: Harris–Stowe State University
description: Formed in 1954 when St. Louis's white Harris Teachers College (1857) merged with Stowe Teachers College, the city's Black teachers college, as the schools desegregated. It is a public HBCU in downtown St. Louis focused on education and business; alumni include federal judge Charles Shaw and anchorman Julius Hunter.

facts.d: HBCU status descends from Stowe Teachers College, merged in 1954.
An African American business leaders council has raised over $400,000 in scholarships for its business program.

sources.label: NewsOne — HBCU spotlight: Harris-Stowe State University

name: Stowe Teachers College
fate: Merged with Harris Teachers College in 1954 to form Harris-Stowe (now Harris–Stowe State University).
description: St. Louis's normal school for Black teachers, begun in connection with Sumner High School and later named for Harriet Beecher Stowe. Its 1954 merger with the white Harris Teachers College is the source of Harris–Stowe's HBCU status.

facts.d: Combined with Harris Teachers College as St. Louis schools desegregated.

name: George R. Smith College
fate: Its building burned on April 26, 1925 and it never reopened; its assets were merged into Philander Smith College in 1933.
description: A Methodist college for Black students in Sedalia, Missouri, named for the town's founder. It operated for three decades until a 1925 fire destroyed it.

facts.d: Burned April 26, 1925.
Merged into Philander Smith College (Little Rock) in 1933.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Reginald F. Lewis
hbcuStory: Won a football scholarship to Virginia State College and earned a B.A. in political science in 1965; a Rockefeller Foundation summer program then led Harvard to invite him to law school.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in East Baltimore, where he quarterbacked Dunbar High School and worked from childhood — famously saying he wanted to 'do business, not just talk about it.'
breakthrough: After 15 years as a corporate lawyer, founded TLC Group in 1983, bought McCall Pattern for $22.5 million and sold it for a large profit, then acquired Beatrice International Foods for $985 million in 1987.
legacy: TLC Beatrice became the first Black-owned company with more than $1 billion in sales; his foundation funded Howard, Harvard Law and Baltimore's Reginald F. Lewis Museum, and VSU's business school carries his name.

breakthroughDetail.d: A $22.5 million buyout he restructured and sold for a large return to investors.
Created TLC Beatrice International Holdings, the first Black-owned company with $1B+ in annual sales.
Forbes listed him among the 400 richest Americans in 1993 with an estimated $400 million.

legacyDetail.d: $1 million to Howard (1988), $3 million to Harvard Law (1992), $5 million toward the Reginald F. Lewis Museum (opened 2005).
After his death from brain cancer at 50, his wife Loida Nicolas Lewis ran TLC Beatrice.

sources.label: VSU College of Business — Alumni (Reginald F. Lewis)

name: Gladys West
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. (1952) and M.S. (1955) in mathematics at Virginia State.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in rural Dinwiddie County, Virginia.
breakthrough: Her modeling of the Earth's shape at the Naval Surface Warfare Center contributed to the development of GPS.
legacy: Inducted into the U.S. Air Force Hall of Fame.

breakthroughDetail.d: Mathematical work contributed to GPS.
Inducted for her contributions.

legacyDetail.d: Celebrated widely only after retirement.

name: Lucy McBath
hbcuStory: Graduated from Virginia State University in 1982.
humbleBeginnings: Daughter of a dentist and NAACP leader in Joliet, Illinois; worked as a Delta Air Lines flight attendant.
breakthrough: After her son Jordan Davis was killed in 2012, became a national gun-safety advocate and was elected to Congress from Georgia.
legacy: Serves as a U.S. Representative from Georgia.

breakthroughDetail.d: U.S. Congresswoman from Georgia.

legacyDetail.d: National spokesperson for gun-violence prevention.

name: William R. Harvey
hbcuStory: Studied at Virginia State (graduate study) after Talladega College, before a Harvard doctorate; then led Hampton University for 44 years.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Brewton, Alabama, in 1941.
breakthrough: Became Hampton's 12th president on July 1, 1978, and in 1986 he and his wife Norma bought a Pepsi-Cola bottling franchise — called the first African American owner in the soft-drink bottling industry.
legacy: Grew Hampton's endowment, campus and research enterprise until retiring June 30, 2022.

breakthroughDetail.d: One of the longest-serving HBCU presidents.
Bought a Pepsi-Cola bottling franchise with his wife Norma.

legacyDetail.d: Expanded Hampton into a research university.

sources.label: AFRO — Dr. William Harvey announces retirement

name: Robert S. Abbott
wealthNote: Widely described as one of the first Black millionaires; no audited figure exists.
hbcuStory: Studied the printing trade at Hampton Institute, finishing in 1896 — the skill that shaped his career.
humbleBeginnings: Born on St. Simons Island, Georgia, to formerly enslaved parents; shut out of Chicago print shops by discrimination, he earned a law degree but couldn't build a practice.
breakthrough: Launched The Chicago Defender in 1905 with an initial investment of 25 cents; it became the most widely circulated Black newspaper in the country and helped propel the Great Migration.
legacy: Paid for his nephew John H. Sengstacke's Hampton education and left him the Defender; also founded Chicago's Bud Billiken Day Parade.

breakthroughDetail.d: Started with 25 cents; became the nation's best-selling Black paper.
The Defender's national circulation urged Southern Black workers north.

legacyDetail.d: Groomed nephew John H. Sengstacke as heir.
Founded Chicago's annual back-to-school parade.

sources.label: PBS The Black Press — Robert Abbott

name: John H. Sengstacke
wealthNote: Estimate based on ownership of the largest Black newspaper chain; no published figure.
hbcuStory: His uncle Robert S. Abbott financed his education at Hampton Institute, where he graduated in 1934 (one record says 1933), working summers at the Defender.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Savannah, Georgia; the son of a minister and editor, he apprenticed in the family newspaper business.
breakthrough: Joined the Defender as vice president and treasurer in 1934, became general manager in 1935 and inherited it on Abbott's death in 1940.
legacy: Built the largest chain of Black newspapers in the U.S. and founded the National Newspaper Publishers Association in 1940, serving seven terms as president.

breakthroughDetail.d: President and editor until his death in 1997.
United Black publishers into a national trade group.

legacyDetail.d: Owned papers including the Defender, Michigan Chronicle, Tri-State Defender and Pittsburgh Courier.

sources.label: PBS The Black Press — John Sengstacke

name: Robert Brokenburr
hbcuStory: Graduated from Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute in 1906, then earned a law degree at Howard University in 1909.
humbleBeginnings: A young Black attorney arriving in Indianapolis at the start of his career.
breakthrough: Wrote the articles of incorporation for the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company in 1911 and, per Wikipedia, served as its general manager and counsel (other sources credit Freeman Ransom as business manager).
legacy: Became the first African American elected to the Indiana State Senate (1940) while maintaining a civil-rights litigation practice.

breakthroughDetail.d: Helped Madam C. J. Walker file her incorporation papers.
First Black member of the Indiana State Senate.

legacyDetail.d: Model of the Black business lawyer as company builder.

sources.label: Indiana Historical Society — Madam C. J. Walker Papers addition

name: Percy Creuzot
wealthNote: Estimate based on a multi-unit regional restaurant chain; no published figure.
hbcuStory: After Navy service in World War II, graduated from Hampton Institute in 1949.
humbleBeginnings: A New Orleans native, he came to Houston in 1965 selling class rings and graduation supplies to Black high schools for Herff-Jones.
breakthrough: In 1969 he and his wife Sallie opened a Creole po-boy stand in Houston's Third Ward that pivoted to fried chicken — Frenchy's, earning him the nickname 'the Black Colonel Sanders.'
legacy: Frenchy's became a Houston institution run by the family; son Percy III led the business and son John Creuzot became Dallas County District Attorney.

breakthroughDetail.d: Founded in Houston's Third Ward near Texas Southern University.
Switched from po-boys to Creole fried chicken soon after opening.

legacyDetail.d: Passed to son Percy Creuzot III.

sources.label: ABC13 — Founder of Frenchy's Fried Chicken chain dies
D Magazine — How John Creuzot's dad built Frenchy's

name: Percy Sutton
wealthNote: Estimate based on Inner City Broadcasting holdings; no published figure verified.
hbcuStory: Attended three HBCUs — Prairie View, Tuskegee Institute and Hampton Institute — without taking a degree, then earned a law degree at Brooklyn Law School in 1950.
humbleBeginnings: Youngest of 15 children of a San Antonio educator; served with the Tuskegee Airmen in World War II.
breakthrough: Co-founded Inner City Broadcasting, which in the early 1970s bought New York's WLIB-AM and WBLS-FM, and around 1980–81 bought Harlem's Apollo Theater.
legacy: Malcolm X's lawyer and Manhattan's longest-serving borough president; Black Enterprise calls him a model for multi-generational wealth.

breakthroughDetail.d: Bought WLIB and WBLS — anchors of Black-owned radio.
Bought and restored the Harlem landmark.

legacyDetail.d: Family-run media company passed to son Pierre Sutton.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Percy E. Sutton remains a model for multi-generational wealth

name: Charles Phillips
wealthNote: Estimated from two decades of Oracle/Infor executive compensation and equity; no published net-worth figure.
hbcuStory: Earned an MBA from Hampton University (1986) while serving as a Marine Corps officer, after a computer science degree from the Air Force Academy; later a J.D. from New York Law School.
humbleBeginnings: Son of an Air Force sergeant from Little Rock, Arkansas.
breakthrough: Became a top-ranked Wall Street software analyst at Morgan Stanley, then was recruited by Larry Ellison and named Oracle president within six months (2003–2010).
legacy: As CEO of Infor (2010–2019) built it into a major cloud software company, then became chairman; co-founded the Black Economic Alliance and the tech-investment firm Recognize.

breakthroughDetail.d: Joined 2003; president/co-president through 2010.
Stepped down as CEO in August 2019 to become chairman.

legacyDetail.d: Featured on Hampton's business-school roster of notable alumni.
Co-founded the Black Economic Alliance and tech investment firm Recognize.

sources.label: Encyclopedia of Arkansas — Charles E. Phillips Jr.

name: Sashi Brown
wealthNote: Estimate based on senior pro-sports executive compensation; no published figure.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.A. in mass media from Hampton University in 1998, calling Pirates football and basketball as an analyst and play-by-play announcer; then Harvard Law (2002). Hampton trustee.
humbleBeginnings: Started his career as a lawyer, becoming the Jacksonville Jaguars' senior vice president and lead counsel.
breakthrough: Rose from Jacksonville Jaguars lead counsel to Cleveland Browns EVP of football operations (2013–17) and president of Monumental's Wizards, Mystics and Go-Go.
legacy: Named president of the Baltimore Ravens on April 1, 2022, overseeing all business operations.

breakthroughDetail.d: Succeeded Dick Cass; oversees finance, sales, stadium and communications.
Ran Cleveland's football operations 2013–2017.

legacyDetail.d: Sits on Hampton's Board of Trustees.

sources.label: Baltimore Ravens — Dick Cass to retire, Sashi Brown named successor

name: Rashida Jones
wealthNote: Estimate based on network-president compensation; no published figure.
hbcuStory: Graduated from Hampton University's Scripps Howard School of Journalism (mass media arts) in 2002; now a Hampton trustee.
humbleBeginnings: Began as a local TV news producer before joining NBC News.
breakthrough: Became president of MSNBC effective February 1, 2021 — the first Black executive to lead a major cable news network.
legacy: After MSNBC, became CEO of Piers Morgan's Uncensored network, per Hampton's trustee listing.

breakthroughDetail.d: First African American to run a major cable news network.
Oversaw breaking-news and election coverage before the promotion.

legacyDetail.d: Delivered Hampton's 150th commencement address.

sources.label: Black Enterprise — Rashida Jones to lead MSNBC

name: Keith Leaphart
hbcuStory: Won a scholarship to Hampton University and graduated in 1996 with a biology degree, later earning a D.O./MBA.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Philadelphia's West Oak Lane; ran a commercial cleaning and event-planning business while in medical and business school.
breakthrough: Founded the Leaphart Group and Replica Creative, then the fintech company Philanthropi.
legacy: Chairs the Lenfest Foundation and serves as Secretary-Treasurer of the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission.

breakthroughDetail.d: Replica Creative, the Leaphart Group and Philanthropi.
Practiced at Bryn Mawr Hospital while running businesses.

legacyDetail.d: Chair of the Lenfest Foundation.

name: Michele Jawando
hbcuStory: Earned her bachelor's degree at Hampton University (2002), then a J.D. from UNC Chapel Hill; serves on Hampton's board.
humbleBeginnings: Began on Capitol Hill working for Senator Kirsten Gillibrand.
breakthrough: Moved to Google's public policy team, then to Omidyar Network as SVP of programs before being named CEO.
legacy: Leads one of the best-known philanthropic investment firms in tech.

breakthroughDetail.d: Heads Pierre Omidyar's social-change investment firm.
Managed relationships with nonprofits and policymakers.

legacyDetail.d: Listed on Hampton's Board of Trustees.

name: Nicole Pullen Ross
wealthNote: Estimate based on Goldman Sachs partner compensation; no published figure.
hbcuStory: Hampton University class of 1994; vice chair of Hampton's Board of Trustees.
humbleBeginnings: Built her career inside Goldman Sachs's private wealth business.
breakthrough: Became a Goldman Sachs partner and head of the Northeast Private Wealth Management region and of Sports & Entertainment Solutions.
legacy: Uses her board role to steer Hampton's governance and alumni finance network.

breakthroughDetail.d: Northeast Private Wealth Management region head.
Heads the firm's Sports & Entertainment Solutions group.

legacyDetail.d: Vice chair of the Board of Trustees.

sources.label: Hampton University School of Business — Notable Alumni

name: Che Pope
hbcuStory: Hampton University class of 1992, listed among Hampton's notable media alumni.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Boston in 1970; came up as a record producer.
breakthrough: Spent about eight years on Dr. Dre's Aftermath production team (Eminem, 50 Cent), then served as president and COO of Kanye West's GOOD Music (2012–2015).
legacy: Founded the content company Wrkshp Media.

breakthroughDetail.d: Ran the label's operations 2012–2015.
Produced for Eminem and 50 Cent.

legacyDetail.d: Built his own media company.

name: Booker T. Washington
hbcuStory: Walked much of the 500 miles to Hampton Institute, worked as a janitor to pay his way and graduated in 1875 under Samuel Chapman Armstrong; also studied at Wayland Seminary (1878–79).
humbleBeginnings: Born enslaved in Virginia; worked in West Virginia salt furnaces and coal mines as a boy.
breakthrough: Became the first principal of Tuskegee Institute in 1881 and, in 1900, founded the National Negro Business League.
legacy: Built Tuskegee into a national institution and networked Black entrepreneurs through the NNBL; Hampton remains the model he spread across the South.

breakthroughDetail.d: First leader of Tuskegee Institute.
Organized Black business owners nationally.

legacyDetail.d: Exported Hampton's industrial-education philosophy.

name: James Solomon Russell
hbcuStory: Admitted to Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute in the 1870s, then to Bishop Payne Divinity School in Petersburg in 1878.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Mecklenburg County, Virginia, in 1857.
breakthrough: Founded Saint Paul Normal and Industrial School in 1888 after teaching Black students in a church room from 1883.
legacy: As Archdeacon of Southern Virginia grew Black Episcopal congregations from none to 37; first African American on the Episcopal Board of Missions; commemorated in the Episcopal calendar.

breakthroughDetail.d: Bought the first building with a legacy from the Rev. Saul of Philadelphia.
Planted 37 Black Episcopal churches.

legacyDetail.d: Turned down election as Suffragan Bishop of Arkansas in 1917.

name: Mary Jackson
hbcuStory: Graduated from Hampton Institute in 1942 with degrees in mathematics and physical science.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Hampton, Virginia; taught math and worked as a bookkeeper before NACA.
breakthrough: Became NASA's first Black female engineer at Langley Research Center.
legacy: Awarded a posthumous Congressional Gold Medal; NASA headquarters is named for her.

breakthroughDetail.d: At Langley Research Center.

legacyDetail.d: Recognized posthumously.

name: Wanda Sykes
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in marketing from Hampton University in 1986.
humbleBeginnings: Worked as a contracting specialist at the National Security Agency before stand-up.
breakthrough: Emmy-winning writer, comedian and actor.
legacy: Runs her own production company and is a frequent Hampton ambassador.

breakthroughDetail.d: Won as a writer on The Chris Rock Show.

legacyDetail.d: Owns production company Push It Productions.

sources.label: Hampton University School of Business — Notable Alumni

name: Ruth E. Carter
hbcuStory: Graduated from Hampton University in 1982.
humbleBeginnings: Raised by a single mother in Springfield, Massachusetts.
breakthrough: Won the Academy Award for costume design for Black Panther — and a second Oscar for Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.
legacy: First Black winner in the costume design category.

breakthroughDetail.d: Black Panther and Wakanda Forever.

legacyDetail.d: Longtime costume designer on Spike Lee films.

name: Freeman A. Hrabowski III
hbcuStory: Entered Hampton Institute as a teenager and graduated in 1969 with highest honors in mathematics.
humbleBeginnings: Marched as a child in Birmingham's 1963 Children's Crusade and was jailed.
breakthrough: Led the University of Maryland, Baltimore County as president for three decades, building the Meyerhoff Scholars STEM program.
legacy: Made UMBC a top producer of Black STEM Ph.D.s.

legacyDetail.d: National model for minority STEM achievement.

name: Ernest M. Hodge
wealthNote: Estimate based on ownership of a multi-state dealership group; no published figure.
hbcuStory: Graduated from Norfolk State in 1975 with a business degree; NSU's Ernest M. Hodge Institute for Entrepreneurship is named for him.
humbleBeginnings: Trained at the General Motors Dealer Development Academy in Flint, Michigan.
breakthrough: Built Heritage Automotive Group (Cadillac, VW, Infiniti, Chevrolet stores in Georgia and New York) and became co-CEO of March/Hodge Automotive Group.
legacy: His group ranked first among minority-owned dealerships on Black Enterprise's list; inducted into the National Black College Alumni Hall of Fame.

breakthroughDetail.d: Owner, CEO and president.
Ranked #1 minority-owned auto dealer group by Black Enterprise.

legacyDetail.d: Ernest M. Hodge Institute for Entrepreneurship.

sources.label: NSU — Ernest M. Hodge Institute for Entrepreneurship

name: Derek T. Dingle
hbcuStory: Earned a journalism degree at Norfolk State, later studying magazine management at NYU.
humbleBeginnings: Joined Black Enterprise in 1983 as an assistant editor.
breakthrough: Co-founded Milestone Media in 1993 — the Black-owned comics imprint behind Static — serving as its president and CEO.
legacy: Returned to lead Black Enterprise editorially as editor-in-chief (2008) and later chief content officer.

legacy: His company has removed dozens of monuments across the South despite threats; he sold NFTs of the removals to raise money for charity.

hbcuStory: Earned a Bachelor of Business Administration from Norfolk State College in 1968.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Norfolk, Virginia; worked in corporate sales at DuPont before comedy.

name: Robert L. Vann
hbcuStory: Enrolled in 1901 at Wayland Academy, Virginia Union's preparatory school, and continued at Virginia Union until 1903 before winning a scholarship to the Western University of Pennsylvania.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Hertford County, North Carolina; graduated valedictorian of Waters Training School in 1901.
breakthrough: Became Pitt Law's first Black graduate (1909) and turned the Pittsburgh Courier into the nation's most widely circulated Black newspaper.
legacy: Left bequests that funded scholarships at Virginia Union and the Robert L. Vann Memorial Tower on its campus.

First African American graduate of Pitt's law school, 1909.

name: James H. Blackwell
hbcuStory: Graduated from the Richmond Theological Institute (a Virginia Union predecessor) in 1880 and attended Virginia Union; later earned a Ph.D. at Princeton.
humbleBeginnings: Born into slavery in Marion, Virginia, in 1864; began teaching in 1880.
breakthrough: Founded the Virginia Industrial Mercantile and Building and Loan Association (1891) and the Benevolent Investment and Relief Association (1898), which issued over 12,000 insurance policies to African Americans.
legacy: Also founded Southside Realty and held officer roles at Second Street Savings Bank; Richmond's Blackwell neighborhood and J.H. Blackwell Elementary are named for him.

Benevolent Investment and Relief Association with branches in VA, DC and MD.

Richmond's Blackwell community.

name: Emmett C. Burke
hbcuStory: Earned a bachelor of laws from Virginia Union University in 1926 while already a banker; VUU trustee 1943–1953.
humbleBeginnings: Son of a Richmond laborer; graduated from the Richmond Colored Normal School in 1893 and became a teller at the True Reformers' Bank in 1894.
breakthrough: Cashier of Maggie L. Walker's St. Luke Penny Savings Bank from its 1903 opening; after the 1930 merger he succeeded Walker as president of Consolidated Bank and Trust.
legacy: His conservative lending was credited with carrying the bank through the Great Depression.

Succeeded Maggie L. Walker after the 1930 merger.

hbcuStory: Graduated from Virginia Union in 1961 (M.D., Meharry 1968) and chaired VUU's board of trustees for three decades.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Lynchburg, Virginia, in 1939; practiced family medicine in Richmond from 1969.

legacy: Steered Virginia Union and Meharry as board chair.

Led the National Medical Association.

name: Max Robinson
hbcuStory: Studied at Virginia Union University (listed by VUU as a student and in his Wikipedia infobox) after time at Oberlin.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Richmond, Virginia; served briefly in the Air Force studying Russian at Indiana University.

legacy: Co-founded the National Association of Black Journalists.

name: Randall Robinson
hbcuStory: Studied at Virginia Union University (listed by VUU and in Norfolk State's alumni list), then Harvard Law School.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in segregated Richmond; younger brother of anchor Max Robinson.
breakthrough: Founded TransAfrica, the lobby that drove the Free South Africa Movement and U.S. sanctions against apartheid.
legacy: Author of The Debt, a landmark case for reparations.

name: L. Douglas Wilder
hbcuStory: Graduated from Virginia Union University in 1951 with a degree in chemistry.

name: Samuel L. Gravely Jr.

legacyDetail.d: Vice admiral in command of the Third Fleet.

name: Vernon Johns

humbleBeginnings: Born on a Prince Edward County farm in 1892 and returned to farming between pulpits.

legacy: Succeeded at Dexter by Martin Luther King Jr.; remembered as a forerunner of the civil rights movement.

Predecessor of Martin Luther King Jr.

legacyDetail.d: Urged congregants toward Black economic independence.

name: Raymond V. Haysbert
hbcuStory: After World War II enrolled at Central State and Wilberforce, earning degrees in accounting and mathematics; then taught at Wilberforce.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Cincinnati; served with the Tuskegee Airmen in Africa and Italy.
breakthrough: Joined Baltimore's Parks Sausage Company in 1952 and rose to CEO as it became one of the largest Black-owned businesses and the first to go public.
legacy: National Minority Entrepreneur of the Year (1991); chaired the Greater Baltimore Urban League.

National Minority Entrepreneur of the Year.

legacyDetail.d: Chaired the Greater Baltimore Urban League.

humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Minerva, Ohio; served in World War II with the Army Air Forces and was denied a G.I. loan on return.
breakthrough: With backing from two Black physicians and his brother, bought an Ohio dairy farm and built Clearview Golf Club himself, opening nine holes in the late 1940s.
legacy: Bought out his partners, expanded Clearview to 18 holes in 1978 and kept it in the family; daughter Renee Powell, an LPGA pro, runs it.

hbcuStory: Completed Wilberforce University's secretarial program in 1917 (attended 1915–1917).
humbleBeginnings: Trained as a secretary at a time when few business schools admitted Black women.
breakthrough: Opened Lewis Business College in Indianapolis in January 1928 on a $50 loan and opened a Detroit branch around 1938–39.
legacy: The Detroit school became Lewis College of Business — Michigan's only HBCU — and was revived as Pensole Lewis College in 2021–22; a Michigan highway is named for her.

Opened in Detroit around 1938–39; the Indianapolis school closed in 1940.

1,400 to 23,000+ members.

Caterpillar, FedEx and Allstate.

hbcuStory: Attended Central State University in Ohio, majoring in sociology and playing on the football team.

The Winans, Toni Braxton, R. Kelly.

hbcuStory: Barred from local high school, she enrolled at Western University in Quindaro, Kansas, at 13, studying privately with Will Marion Cook; later earned a degree at Langston University.

Choral director for MGM.

hbcuStory: Studied music at Western University in Quindaro, paying tuition by singing on Topeka radio and the Chautauqua circuit; later a B.A. from the University of Kansas (1931).

Porgy and Bess on Broadway and tour.
